quests.instruction: Swallowing seawater makes you thirstier, because your body needs extra water to flush out the salt. Which organs do the flushing?
quests.hint: They filter your blood and make pee.
quests.explanation: Seawater is much saltier than your body fluids, so your kidneys need extra water to get rid of the salt, and you end up losing water instead of gaining it.
quests.funFact: That is why sailors adrift at sea are told not to drink seawater.

quests.instruction: After a hike through tall grass, a grown-up checks your body for ticks. Which part of you are they inspecting?
quests.hint: Ticks cling to it, often in warm, hidden spots.
quests.explanation: Ticks bite and hold on to the skin, so checking after you have been outdoors helps remove them quickly.
quests.funFact: Ticks like warm, hidden spots such as behind the knees and ears.

quests.instruction: Standing outside during a thunderstorm, you feel your hair stand on end and your skin tingle. Which part is reacting to the electric charge in the air?
quests.hint: It stands up when charged, like after you rub it with a balloon.
quests.explanation: Electric charge builds up before lightning and can make your hair rise. If this happens, tell a grown-up and get indoors right away.
quests.funFact: Lightning is a giant spark of the same static electricity that makes your hair fly up after rubbing a balloon.

quests.instruction: Which light-sensing cells in your retina, named for their shape, let you see colors?
quests.hint: They work best in bright light.
quests.explanation: Cones sense red, green, and blue light, and your brain mixes their signals into all the colors you see.
quests.funFact: Each eye has about six million cones.

quests.instruction: At night, colors look gray because the light-sensing cells that work in dim light cannot see color. What are they called?
quests.hint: They are named for their long, thin shape.
quests.explanation: Rods are very sensitive to dim light but cannot tell colors, so a moonlit garden looks silvery gray.
quests.funFact: Each eye has about a hundred million rods.

quests.instruction: There is a tiny patch in each eye where you cannot see anything, because the optic nerve leaves the retina there. What is it called?
quests.hint: It has no light-sensing cells.
quests.explanation: Where the optic nerve attaches, there are no light-sensing cells, so that spot cannot see. Your brain fills in the missing piece.
quests.funFact: You can find your blind spot by closing one eye and watching a dot slide out of sight at the side of your vision.

quests.instruction: When you have a cold, your face feels heavy because air-filled spaces in your skull behind your forehead and cheeks fill with mucus. What are they called?
quests.hint: They are hollow spaces in the bones of your face.
quests.explanation: Sinuses are hollow spaces in your skull. They are lined with mucus, and when you have a cold, they can fill up and feel stuffy.
quests.funFact: Sinuses make your skull lighter and help give your voice its sound.

quests.instruction: When you have a cold, you can feel small, tender lumps in your neck. These tiny bean-shaped filters trap germs. What are they?
quests.hint: You can feel them swell under your jaw.
quests.explanation: Lymph nodes filter fluid and hold white blood cells that attack germs, so they can swell when you are fighting an infection.
quests.funFact: Your body has hundreds of lymph nodes.

quests.instruction: Which tiny skin parts make the oily coating that keeps skin and hair soft, but can clog and cause pimples?
quests.hint: They open into the same tiny pockets as hairs.
quests.explanation: Oil glands release a natural oil that protects the skin, and when a pore gets blocked, a pimple can form.
quests.funFact: Oil glands become more active in the teen years, which is why many teens get pimples.

quests.instruction: As people get older, which part of the body slowly loses some of its stretchiness and develops wrinkles?
quests.hint: Lotion and sun protection help look after it.
quests.explanation: Over many years, skin makes less of the stretchy fibers that keep it smooth, so it forms wrinkles.
quests.funFact: Protecting your skin from the sun throughout life helps slow wrinkles.

quests.instruction: Each hair on your body grows out of a tiny pocket in the skin. What is it called?
quests.hint: It is the hair's home, and it holds the root.
quests.explanation: A follicle is a tiny pocket in the skin where a hair grows from its root.
quests.funFact: You have about five million hair follicles, and most of them are on your body, not your head.

quests.instruction: Look closely at your fingertip. Which fingerprint pattern looks like a spiral or a swirl?
quests.hint: Think of a tiny whirlpool.
quests.explanation: Fingerprints come in three main patterns: loops, arches, and whorls. A whorl swirls around in circles.
quests.funFact: No two people, not even identical twins, have exactly the same fingerprints.

quests.instruction: Deep in your brain is a small, curved part shaped like a seahorse that helps turn new experiences into memories. What is it called?
quests.hint: Its name means seahorse.
quests.explanation: The hippocampus helps you store new memories, like what you did today or where you left your shoes.
quests.funFact: Taxi drivers who learn a big city's streets by heart often have a larger hippocampus.

quests.instruction: During dreaming sleep, your big muscles stay very still so you do not act out your dreams. Which part at the base of the brain tells them to stay still?
quests.hint: It also keeps your breathing going.
quests.explanation: The brain stem sends signals that keep most muscles relaxed during dreaming sleep, which is why you stay in bed.
quests.funFact: Dreaming sleep is called REM sleep, which stands for rapid eye movement.

quests.instruction: A newborn baby sees best at about the distance of a parent's face when held in arms. Which part of the baby is still learning to focus on far-off things?
quests.hint: They get better at seeing far away over the first months.
quests.explanation: A newborn's vision is blurry, and babies see faces and bold patterns best when they are close.
quests.funFact: Babies like to look at faces and at high-contrast patterns, such as black and white stripes.

quests.instruction: Reading in a car can make you feel sick when your eyes say "still" but a part of your ear says "moving." Which part senses the motion?
quests.hint: It has fluid-filled loops that sense movement.
quests.explanation: Fluid in the loops of the inner ear sloshes when you move, and the brain compares that message with what your eyes see. When they do not match, you can feel sick.
quests.funFact: Looking out the window at the far horizon can help.

quests.instruction: Hot chili peppers feel burning hot even though they are not really hot. Which parts in your mouth are being fooled into sending a heat message?
quests.hint: They carry messages to your brain.
quests.explanation: Chili peppers contain a chemical that triggers the nerves that sense heat, so your brain thinks your mouth is burning.
quests.funFact: Milk helps with spicy food better than water does.

quests.instruction: After eating garlic, your breath can smell even after you brush your teeth, because the smell goes into your blood and is breathed out from which parts?
quests.hint: They add oxygen to your blood and remove other gases.
quests.explanation: Smelly substances from garlic enter your blood and travel to the lungs, where they leave your body with every breath.
quests.funFact: Brushing helps, but garlic breath can last until your body has cleared the smelly substances.

quests.instruction: An X-ray picture shows which parts clearly, because they block more of the rays than soft parts do?
quests.hint: They look white in the picture.
quests.explanation: X-rays pass easily through soft parts but are blocked by dense bones, so bones show up as white.
quests.funFact: The first X-ray picture, taken in 1895, showed the bones of a hand.

quests.instruction: A bruise turns purple, then green, then yellow as it heals. What is slowly changing color under the skin?
quests.hint: It leaked out of tiny vessels.
quests.explanation: A bruise is blood that has leaked from tiny vessels and is trapped under the skin. As the body breaks it down, its color changes.
quests.funFact: Most bruises fade away in about two weeks.

quests.instruction: After you recover from an infection or get a vaccine, your body keeps special proteins ready to fight that same germ again. What are they called?
quests.hint: They fit a germ like a key fits a lock.
quests.explanation: Antibodies are made by the immune system. They recognize particular germs and help destroy them.
quests.funFact: Some antibodies stay in your body for years, and some for a lifetime.

quests.instruction: Most of the nutrients from your food pass into your blood through the walls of which long, coiled tube?
quests.hint: It comes right after the stomach.
quests.explanation: The small intestine absorbs nutrients through its walls into the blood, and what is left moves on to the large intestine.
quests.funFact: Its inner wall is covered in tiny finger-like bumps called villi, which give it a huge surface for absorbing food.

quests.instruction: Tiny parts inside your cells turn food and oxygen into energy and are nicknamed the cell's powerhouses. What are they called?
quests.hint: A muscle cell has lots of them.
quests.explanation: Mitochondria release energy from food using oxygen, which powers everything your cells do.
quests.funFact: Muscle and heart cells have many mitochondria, because they need lots of energy.

quests.instruction: When you run, your heart speeds up, you breathe faster, and you sweat, all without deciding to. Which part of the nervous system runs these automatic jobs?
quests.hint: It works on its own, in the background.
quests.explanation: The autonomic nervous system controls heart rate, breathing, digestion, and sweating without you thinking about it.
quests.funFact: It also controls how wide your pupils open.

quests.instruction: All of your body parts are built from tiny living units that are too small to see without a microscope. What are they called?
quests.hint: Under a microscope, they look like tiny rooms.
quests.explanation: Your body is made of trillions of cells, and each one is alive.
quests.funFact: An adult has roughly thirty to forty trillion cells.

quests.instruction: Cells of the same kind that work together, such as muscle cells or nerve cells, form what?
quests.hint: They are the next step up from cells.
quests.explanation: Groups of similar cells make up tissue, such as muscle tissue, nerve tissue, and skin tissue.
quests.funFact: The human body has four main kinds of tissue: muscle, nerve, connective, and the lining kind called epithelial.

quests.instruction: Different tissues that team up to do one big job, like the heart pumping blood, make up what?
quests.hint: The heart, stomach, and lungs are examples.
quests.explanation: An organ is made of several kinds of tissue working together. The stomach, for example, has muscle, nerve, and lining tissue.
quests.funFact: Some organs can be replaced with a transplant from a donor.

quests.instruction: Groups of organs that work together on a big job, like the stomach and intestines digesting food, make up what?
quests.hint: The digestive system is an example.
quests.explanation: An organ system links several organs together, such as the digestive system or the circulatory system.
quests.funFact: Organ systems rely on each other: the lungs bring in oxygen, the heart delivers it, and the kidneys clean the blood.

quests.instruction: Inside almost every cell is a long set of instructions that helps decide things like your eye color. What is it called?
quests.hint: It is shaped like a twisted ladder.
quests.explanation: DNA carries your body's instructions, which you inherit from your parents.
quests.funFact: If you stretched out the DNA from a single cell, it would be about two meters long.

quests.instruction: Lymph nodes, tonsils, and the spleen belong to a system that drains extra fluid and helps fight germs. What is it called?
quests.hint: It is a partner of the immune system.
quests.explanation: The lymphatic system collects fluid that leaks from blood vessels and carries it back, while its nodes filter out germs.
quests.funFact: Unlike blood, lymph has no heart to pump it, so it moves along as your muscles squeeze.
